newsitem.title: USA: Senate sets confirmation hearing for Vietnam envoy.
newsitem.headline: Senate sets confirmation hearing for Vietnam envoy.

text.p: Senate confirmation hearings for President Bill Clinton's nominee to be the first U.S. ambassador to Vietnam will begin next Thursday despite a last-ditch effort by key House Republicans to delay them, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee said on Thursday.
Clinton's nominee is former Representative Pete Peterson, a retired Air Force fighter pilot held as a prisoner of war for six-and-a-half years after his aircraft was shot down near Hanoi in 1966.
If confirmed as expected, Peterson, who served in the House of Representatives as a Florida Democrat from 1991 until last year, would become the first U.S. ambassador in a united Vietnam.
Previous U.S. ambassadors were accredited to the U.S.-backed South Vietnamese government in Saigon that was overrun by the Communist-ruled North in April 1975.
After years of friction over the more than 2,000 U.S. servicemen listed as missing from the war, President Bill Clinton established diplomatic relations with Vietnam in July 1995.

But unanswered questions about the fate of some of those men have kept relations on a slow track, with normal trade status yet to be worked out. The appointment of an ambassador probably would give a new shot in the arm to economic normalisation, U.S. officials have said.
The U.S. embassy in Hanoi is headed by Desaix Anderson, a career foreign service official with the title of charge d'affaires.

The chairman of the House Committee on International Relations and three colleagues had urged in a letter on Wednesday that confirmation hearings be postponed until completion of congressional probes into whether U.S. policy toward Vietnam had been improperly influenced by illegal foreign financial contributions to President Clinton's re-election effort.

They cited probes into the Commerce Department's advocacy of normalisation, "which appears to have been actively coordinated in violation of conflict of interest regulations" by John Huang, a top Democratic National Committee fundraiser who worked for the Lippo Group of Indonesia before becoming deputy assistant secretary of commerce.
Lippo, with extensive business interests at stake, was eager for the United States to normalise ties with Vietnam.

A spokesman for Senator Jesse Helms, the North Carolina Republican who chairs the Foreign Relations Committee, did not immediately return a phone call seeking comment on the decision to go ahead with the hearing despite the request from his House counterpart, Ben Gilman of New York.

In their letters to Helms and to Craig Thomas, the Wyoming Republican who heads the subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific, Gilman and his colleagues said it was "imperative for Congress and the American people to know whether or not U.S. foreign policy toward Vietnam is wholly, or in part, the result of illegal foreign financial contributions."

"We strongly believe it would be irresponsible for the Senate to now begin action, at the president's request, to confirm an ambassador to Vietnam," added the letter, which was also signed by Gerald Solomon of New York, chairman of the House Rules Committee; Dan Burton of Indiana, chair of the Committee on Government Reform; and Sam Johnson of Texas, a member of the U.S.-Russian Joint Commission on POW/MIAs (prisoners of war/missing in action).

Thomas, the subcommittee chair, said in reply that he shared the letter writers' concerns that, Clinton administration claims notwithstanding, Vietnam "is not fully cooperating with us on the POW/MIA issue."

"And I am worried because some of the president's actions appear to put his administration's political and economic agenda ahead of our missing servicemen, who should be our absolute highest priority in dealing with Vietnam," Thomas said in a letter to Gilman.

But he said he favoured holding at least the initial confirmation hearing. He said he would use it to ask Peterson and the administration "very pertinent and specific questions" about the MIA issues as well as the campaign contributions and any Vietnam policy link.

If confirmed as expected, Peterson would become the first U.S. ambassador in Hanoi. Previous U.S. envoys were accredited to the U.S.-backed South Vietnamese government in Saigon that was overrun by Communist-ruled North Vietnam and southern communist guerrilla forces in April 1975.
After years of friction over unanswered questions about the fate of more than 2,000 U.S. servicemen listed as missing from the war, Clinton established diplomatic relations with Vietnam in July 1995.

But remaining questions about the fate of some missing servicemen have kept relations on a slow track. Appointment of an ambassador would probably give a new boost to economic normalisation, U.S. officials have said.

The chairman of the House Committee on International Relations and three colleagues had urged in a letter on Wednesday that confirmation hearings be postponed until completion of congressional probes into whether U.S. policy toward Vietnam had been improperly influenced by illegal foreign financial contributions to Clinton's 1996 reelection effort.
